note: Every layer and reading in CAIRN, with the mission, instrument, product and provider it came from.

entries.layer: Terrain elevation (3D surface, slope, routing grid)
entries.product: HiRISE DTM DTEEC_019698_1750_019988_1750_U01 (1 m/post), 'Lower northwest portion of mound in Gale Crater'
entries.provider: HiRISE team, University of Arizona (NASA PDS)
entries.usedFor: 3D terrain mesh (2 m), per-pixel relief lighting (1 m), slope map, metabolic cost of every step, impassable-ground mask, terrain shielding

entries.provider: HiRISE team, University of Arizona (NASA PDS)
entries.usedFor: Ground texture at 25 cm, sand-ripple detection
entries.note: HiRISE is a single-band (grey) image here; the Mars colour in the 3D view is a display tint.

entries.product: The same HiRISE DTM at 20 m and orthoimage ESP_019698_1750_RED_C_01_ORTHO (1 m/px) over 6.8 km
entries.provider: HiRISE team, University of Arizona (NASA PDS)
entries.usedFor: Terrain around the walk area in 3D and the regional map in the briefing
entries.note: Outside the HiRISE strip the surroundings are filled with the nearest edge values and fade out.

entries.product: THEMIS Night IR controlled mosaic, global v2 (October 2018), 100 m/px — THEMIS_NightIR_ControlledMosaics_100m_v2_oct2018, WMTS tiles
entries.provider: NASA Mars Trek (Solar System Treks Project, NASA Ames) / Arizona State University
entries.usedFor: Thermal layer; fused with HiRISE to flag loose sand (sand is cold at night, bedrock stays warm)
entries.note: Native resolution is 100 m, so this layer is smooth at walking scale. Trek's tiles were shifted 75 m west and 84 m north to match the USGS controlled mosaic, measured at Jezero where both exist.

entries.instrument: HiRISE image, HiRISE DTM, THEMIS night IR
entries.product: Computed by CAIRN (data-pipeline/build_site.py): ripple texture in the HiRISE image and DTM, weighted by THEMIS night-time temperature
entries.credit: Derived from NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona data
entries.usedFor: Extra walking energy on sand (×2.1 at full strength) and slower walking speed
entries.note: This is our own analysis, not an official NASA product.

entries.product: Computed by CAIRN: share of the sky blocked by terrain within 260 m, weighted by a cos² zenith dependence of the surface dose
entries.credit: Derived from NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona data
entries.usedFor: Sky shielding layer, dose along the route, nearest natural cover during the storm
entries.note: Model, not a measurement: the zenith exponent is an assumption.

entries.usedFor: Position of every EVA stop, the rover track on the map, and the regional traverse

entries.product: MSL raw images feed — images taken at the same rover positions (or sols) as the EVA stops
entries.usedFor: "What you will see" photos and the 360° panoramas

entries.product: REMS calibrated environmental record (MODRDR), sol 4605: ambient air temperature, ground brightness temperature, pressure
entries.provider: NASA Planetary Data System, Atmospheres Node
entries.usedFor: Pressure, air temperature and ground temperature readouts during the EVA

entries.product: MSL-M-RAD-3-RDR-V1.0, sols 4189–4194 (18–24 May 2024), detector E dose rate
entries.provider: NASA Planetary Data System, Planetary Plasma Interactions Node
entries.usedFor: Background dose rate and the measured points of the storm replay
entries.note: Measured by Curiosity itself, about 2.3 km from this walk area (Gediz Vallis, sols 4189–4194). The archive holds 2–4 hours of dosimetry per sol, so the first ~13 hours of the 20 May 2024 storm are filled by a clearly labelled model scaled to NASA's reported 8,100 micrograys.

entries.instrument: DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information)
entries.provider: NASA CCMC / Moon to Mars Space Weather Analysis Office
entries.usedFor: The real eruption record and alert text shown in the storm replay
Global locator in the mission briefing
